artifacts.title: Mr. & Mrs. Matthew Bernard v. Ascension Presbytery..p. 224
artifacts.synopsis: Appeal by Mr. and Mrs. Matthew Bernard against an excommunication censure imposed by the Session of Church of the Savior, Williamsville, New York (a Commission of Presbytery appointed by Ascension Presbytery). The Standing Judicial Commission determined the appeal was administratively out of order because it had not been heard by the next higher court (Ascension Presbytery) before being brought to the General Assembly. The Commission held that appeals must go to the next higher court, not the court of original jurisdiction.

artifacts.title: Reference from Central Carolina Presbytery
artifacts.synopsis: The Standing Judicial Commission declined to adjudicate a reference from Central Carolina Presbytery regarding complaints by William A. Conrad against the Interim Session of Prosperity Presbyterian Church. The panel found that additional related complaints had been lodged that were not formally referred to the Commission, and adjudicating the referred matters would render these additional complaints moot without giving them proper consideration under BCO 41-5. The case was referred back to the Central Carolina Presbytery.

artifacts.title: Morse v. Covenant Presbytery
artifacts.synopsis: The Standing Judicial Commission addressed three issues regarding actions of Covenant Presbytery involving TE Daniel R. Morse and Grace Presbyterian Church. The Commission ruled that teaching elders Morse and Crenshaw, having renounced communion with the PCA by joining the Reformed Episcopal Church, should be removed from presbytery rolls under BCO 38-3. The Commission found no provision requiring churches to notify presbytery before withdrawing from the PCA. Finally, the Commission determined that receiving and recording a protest is an administrative act, not a judicial decision, and that complaints regarding such actions are barred by BCO 45-5.

artifacts.title: Nickoley and Stephens v. Southwest Presbytery
artifacts.synopsis: Bruce Nickoley and David Stephens complained against Southwest Presbytery's actions in withdrawing charges against two ruling elders, dissolving a pastoral relationship, and rescinding its suspension of a local church session. The SJC denied the complaint, affirming that the Presbytery correctly determined it lacked constitutional authority to suspend the session or act as a 'Session pro tem' without congregational consent, and that original jurisdiction over charges against ruling elders rested with the local session.
